passage:
Asif was eleven, on his mother's phone after homework. He had asked his friend Vinita, "Can I borrow your cricket cards for Saturday?" The reply came in a second: "ok".
Only two letters, no smiley, no "sure!" Asif stared at it. Vinita was angry about the torn card last week, he thought. His stomach felt heavy. He typed "sorry" and deleted it.
"What's wrong?" asked Amma, folding clothes nearby.
"Vinita said ok. Just ok."
"Ask her, then."
Asif typed, "Are you angry with me?" A minute later: "no silly!! I was doing dance steps, thumbs only 😄"
Asif laughed and let out a long breath.

qa.q: What did Vinita write in reply to the request about cricket cards?
qa.a: Vinita wrote "ok".

qa.q: Why did Asif's stomach feel heavy after reading Vinita's reply?
qa.a: Asif was worried that Vinita was angry about the torn card. The short "ok" had no smiley, so Asif read it through that fear.

qa.q: What did Asif do that cleared up the worry?
qa.a: Asif asked Vinita straight out whether Vinita was angry. Vinita answered that the reply was short because of dance steps and thumbs only.

qa.q: Why might Vinita have written such a short reply?
qa.a: Vinita was busy doing dance steps and typing with thumbs only, so a quick "ok" was all that fit. It was not meant to show anger.

grounding: A child reads a short "ok" from a friend as anger, then checks and learns the friend was busy.

passage:
"Ganga, why are you angry with me?" Tarun stood by the school bus, backpack half open.
"I'm not!"
"You wrote 'k'. Only 'k'. You are my best friend and you always write 'okay okay okay!'"
Ganga blinked. "I was on the bus stairs. I was holding my bag with one hand. I only had space for one letter."
"But it looked cross."
"It looked cross because you read it in a cross voice," Ganga said, and giggled. "I'm happy. I got the last mango bar today."
Tarun let out a laugh. "Next time write two letters, okay?"
"Okay okay okay!" said Ganga, and held out half the bar.

qa.q: What single letter did Ganga send in the message?
qa.a: Ganga wrote "k".

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when Tarun asked Ganga why Ganga was angry?
qa.a: Tarun was worried and unsure, because Ganga usually wrote "okay okay okay!" and the lone "k" looked cross. Tarun needed to hear it out loud.

qa.q: What could Tarun try when a short message feels cold?
qa.a: Tarun could ask the friend directly, as Tarun did at the bus. Asking in person or by call lets the voice and face show how the friend really feels.

qa.q: How did Ganga see the message "k" when it was written?
qa.a: Ganga saw it as just a fast reply typed with one hand on the bus stairs. Ganga did not know the letter would look cross to Tarun.

grounding: A child reads a friend's short "k" as anger, and the friend explains it was just a rushed message.

passage:
"Didi, Jyoti's angry with me."
"Why?"
"I asked if she wants to come to my building for cycling tomorrow. She wrote only 'ok'. No smiley, nothing."
"Maybe 'ok' means okay, Omkar."
"She always sends three smileys. Today, two letters. I think it's because I didn't pick her in the relay."
"Did she say that?"
"No, but—"
"Then call her. Here, use my phone."
"Hello, Jyoti? It's Omkar. Are you... angry?"
"Angry? No! I was eating and Mummy said no phone at dinner, so I typed fast. I'm coming at five. Should I bring my helmet?"
"Yes! Bring it!"
"Why did you think I was angry?"
"Your 'ok' looked angry."
"Ha! My 'ok' was hungry."
Omkar handed back the phone, grinning. "Didi, she's coming at five."
"See? Two letters can't be angry by themselves."

qa.q: What did Jyoti write back to Omkar?
qa.a: She wrote only "ok", with no smiley.

qa.q: Why did Omkar think Jyoti was angry?
qa.a: Omkar was worried and guilty about not picking Jyoti in the relay, so a short "ok" without her usual smileys looked like anger.

qa.q: What helped Omkar, and what could Omkar try next time?
qa.a: Calling Jyoti to ask cleared it up at once; next time Omkar could ask a quick question like "Are you okay?" before deciding someone is angry.

qa.q: How did Jyoti see her own message?
qa.a: Jyoti saw it as a quick reply typed during dinner and was surprised and amused that it looked angry, joking that her "ok" was hungry 😊

grounding: A child reads a friend's short okay as anger because of an anxious guess, and a call shows it was not.

passage:
This happened when I was in Class 5. My name is Parul, and I had made a card for Gurpreet's birthday party invitation list. I texted from Mama's phone: "Can you come to my house Sunday to make the cards?"
Gurpreet wrote back: "k."
Just one letter and a dot. I stared at it for a long time. I thought maybe Gurpreet was still upset about the lunch box I dropped, or thought my cards were babyish. I didn't sleep well. I even told Mama I didn't want to make cards anymore.
Mama said, "Ask her tomorrow."
At school Gurpreet ran up and said, "I'm coming Sunday! Sorry I wrote so small, my brother was grabbing the phone."
I felt silly and happy at the same time. Now when a message is tiny, I remember that tiny can just mean busy.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet write back to Parul?
qa.a: Gurpreet wrote back "k.", just one letter and a dot.

qa.q: What was Parul worried about after reading the reply?
qa.a: Parul was anxious that Gurpreet was upset about the dropped lunch box or thought the cards were babyish, and felt so hurt that sleep came badly.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who gets a very short message like this?
qa.a: Wait and ask the friend in a kind way, as Mama suggested, before deciding the friend is angry.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet see the message?
qa.a: Gurpreet saw it as a rushed reply while the brother grabbed the phone, and was excited about Sunday, not angry at all.

grounding: A child reads a friend's one-letter reply as anger through the narrator's own fears, and learns short can mean busy.

passage:
After-school centre note, Tuesday
Yusuf came to the reading corner at 4:15, holding the centre tablet, and would not start his worksheet. He showed me the class group message. He had asked Tenzin if they could be partners for the science model, and Tenzin had replied "ok". Yusuf's lip was shaking. "He only writes ok when he's cross," he said. "He's cross because I laughed at his drawing."
I asked what else Tenzin might mean. Yusuf thought for a while and said, "Maybe he's just busy?" I suggested he ask Tenzin in person tomorrow.
Wednesday: Yusuf came in smiling. Tenzin had said yes, he wants to be partners, and he had typed fast because the bus was leaving. Yusuf told me, "I thought his ok had a cross face."
Next step: I will do a short group talk on how messages can't show faces.

qa.q: When did Yusuf come to the reading corner?
qa.a: Yusuf came to the reading corner at 4:15.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when he showed the message?
qa.a: Yusuf was upset and guilty, believing Tenzin was cross about the drawing, which is why his lip was shaking and he would not start his worksheet.

qa.q: What did the adult do well in this situation?
qa.a: The adult asked Yusuf what else Tenzin might mean and suggested asking in person, letting Yusuf find the other explanation himself.

qa.q: How did Tenzin see the reply?
qa.a: Tenzin was simply rushing for the bus and did want to be partners, so he had no idea his "ok" looked cross.

grounding: An adult's note shows a child reading a friend's short okay as anger through his own guilt, then learning otherwise.

passage:
Thursday. Pranav's diary. PRIVATE!!
After school I messaged Pankaj: "Can I borrow your cricket bat on Saturday? Mine's cracked."
He wrote back: "ok"
Just ok. No "sure", no smiley, nothing. Pankaj ALWAYS sends a thumbs up. So I think he's angry about Tuesday, when I didn't pick him for my team in PE. I felt sick all through dinner and didn't finish my dal. I kept typing sorry and deleting it.
Later: Mummy said just ask him. So I called. Pankaj was eating and his mum was shouting at him to hurry for tuition, so he typed with one thumb. He isn't angry at all! He even said I can keep the bat till Sunday.
Next time I'll call before I spend a whole dinner worrying.

qa.q: What did Pranav want to borrow?
qa.a: Pranav wanted to borrow Pankaj's cricket bat on Saturday.

qa.q: Why did Pranav feel sick at dinner?
qa.a: Pranav was worried and guilty, afraid that the short "ok" meant Pankaj was angry about not being picked in PE.

qa.q: What could Pranav do the next time a message seems cold?
qa.a: Call, or send a quick friendly "all good?", before deciding what the message means 🙂

qa.q: What was going on for Pankaj when he typed "ok"?
qa.a: Pankaj was eating and being hurried for tuition, so he typed with one thumb; he was not angry at all and was happy to lend the bat.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's short "ok" as anger because of an earlier worry, until a call shows the friend was just busy.
